Broadcasting a password automatically to different contacts is never a good idea. It makes as simple thing more complex and offers just so many possibilities for a security breach while offering only minimal gain.

  • There might be technical means to intercept the password
  • There might be technical means for an attacker to pretend to be a facebook friend
  • Maybe you don't want that a certain person in your contacts has access to your wifi anymore

This obviously not a privacy apocalypse, but I think it gives reasons for concern.

I just read from this thread that most Americans think newspapers are biased. Do you know any newspapers or -sources that really try to be as unbiased as possible?

Also general tip: if you want to research a topic go read articles from different newspapers (even better if they are from different parts of the world, like the Russian or Brazilian POV).
Do you think there are unbiased newspapers? If yes, which ones?
I'm pretty sure all media is biased in some way. It just depends on who's paying their meal ticket or what their leadership's affiliations are.
In a way you're right but there should be some newspapers whose values are to be unbiased (and they mean it).

Newspapers are often biased because the editors are professionals in the editing field, not in the field they are writing about.

For example, you can't expect an accurate representation of technical news from a mainstream newspaper, where the same editor will write about a new restaurant the next day, and about a new law after that.

Their job is to sell newspapers, not to scare away readers with highly technical details. Besides, editors have no incentives to research a subject deeper than needed to write a couple paragraphs about it.

Truth resists simplicity.

If you want as little bias as possible, go for specialized sources: blogs, reviews, etc.

That's true, but sometimes you also want an overview of the news before digging deeper. Everyone has a bias so most news articles will be biased in some way, but I think the best you can do is read multiple people's point of view. At some point you'll probably find one whose bias swings slightly to your preferred area.

I find in Australia the ABC (state-owned) is the most balanced source of news, but it probably does swing a little left-wing, which I happen to usually agree with.

I agree with your view on editors but your point on specialized sources looks wrong. In blogs people share their POV on various topics, it doesn't seem to try to present the facts of what happened unless they specialize in that.

Also, what blogs do you follow?

In the UK, The Independent has always claimed to be free from political bias and they're probably the closest that comes to it, though they tend to have a liberal stance. The Guardian's also a good one - you probably know them as the newspaper that broke the Edward Snowden stories.

To be honest though, every single news source you find is going to be biased in some way, so the best thing to do is read about the same story from multiple sources and attempt to find a bias-free conclusion from the facts they all present.
